#6276. Scientists turned liquid carbon dioxide into an ice-like solid nearly a mile below the ocean surface

In a South China Sea trial, researchers turned liquid CO₂ into an ice-like solid that was still visible on the seabed 40 days later.

Nearly 1,700 meters below the South China Sea, researchers have turned liquid carbon dioxide into an ice-like solid. A mound remained visible 40 days later, offering an early test of a possible new carbon storage method.

China National Offshore Oil Corporation and Huairou Laboratory carried out the experiment in November 2025. Shouwei Zhou and Junlong Zhu describe it as the first exploratory sea trial of deep-water CO₂ hydrate solidification and storage.

The team injected 70 tons of liquid CO₂ across two wells in the Qiongdongnan Sea Area. They wanted to see whether the deep ocean’s natural cold and pressure could help hold the carbon in solid form.

Capturing carbon dioxide is only part of the job. Keeping it out of the atmosphere requires somewhere to put it, with confidence that it will stay there.

Conventional geological storage involves injecting CO₂ underground, including into formations containing salty water. Before injection begins, engineers must assess the rock, possible escape routes, and the layers expected to seal the reservoir.

The new approach seeks to reduce that dependence on geological seals. Under suitable conditions, CO₂ combines with water to form a hydrate, a solid whose water molecules enclose the gas.

It looks like ice but is neither ordinary frozen water nor dry ice. The researchers’ aim is to form this material beneath the sea and let the surrounding conditions keep it stable.

The deep ocean supplies two conditions that would otherwise have to be created: low temperatures and high pressure.

Those conditions favor hydrate formation. Rather than simply pumping CO₂ into a space where it remains mobile, the team wants it to accumulate as a solid.

The idea draws on work with natural gas hydrates, which contain methane. Extracting gas from those deposits means overcoming the conditions that keep them solid.

For carbon storage, the researchers want the opposite result. A material that stays solid and remains in place could be useful precisely because it is difficult to release.

They identify loose muddy silt and weakly cemented sand-and-mud layers as promising settings for injection and hydrate accumulation.

The operation used the “SS Amazonia” deep-water platform. Beneath it lay 1,696.5 meters of water, with the target reservoir reported at 119 meters below the seabed.

Liquid CO₂ was injected through two wells, LS18-1-C1 and LS18-1-C2. The trial brought together drilling, injection control and underwater monitoring equipment.

During the observed release, the liquid passed through tubing and a nozzle containing several openings. The nozzle dispersed it into small droplets, helping it make contact with seawater.

White hydrate composite particles formed around the drill column. The account calls the cloud of newly formed material “ice mist”.

That was the immediate result. The follow-up inspection would show what could still be seen after several weeks in the deep sea.

Forty days later, images from a remotely operated vehicle showed an accumulated hydrate body on the bottom. Its visible height ranged from 2 to 30 centimeters above the seabed.

The researchers describe it as an artificial CO₂ hydrate “iceberg”. The name is striking, although the formation was a low mound rather than a floating mass.

Finding solid material after 40 days takes the demonstration beyond an instant of successful chemistry. It shows that an accumulation remained visible well after injection.

But the images do not tell us how much of the injected CO₂ was retained in that mound or elsewhere. Nor can a 40-day observation establish whether the carbon will remain contained over much longer periods.

Those are questions for further measurements, rather than conclusions the photographs can supply.

Sensors near the operation measured seawater pH and CO₂ concentrations. The team reported pH holding near 7.4, without unusual spikes in carbon dioxide.

The readings suggest the monitored water experienced little disturbance during the trial. Equipment mounted on the underwater vehicle helped track conditions during injection and release.

That is useful evidence from a first experiment. Still, the absence of a detected change nearby is narrower than proof that the technique has no environmental impact.

A larger operation would need monitoring over a wider area and a longer period. Researchers would also need to establish how the stored material behaves and whether surrounding marine life is affected.

The researchers see potential savings in a method that needs fewer specific geological features. If suitable sites are widespread, finding storage locations could become easier.

They also propose reducing some of the evaluation and infrastructure demands associated with conventional storage.

For now, those are expected advantages rather than commercial results demonstrated by the trial.

The work establishes a preliminary engineering system, including drilling in soft sediments, controlled injection and several kinds of underwater observation. It gives the team something concrete to build on.

The remaining questions concern the carbon itself: how much becomes hydrate, how much stays contained, and how conditions change with larger injections.

Costs will also have to include getting captured CO₂ to the offshore site.

The seabed mound is a promising start. Turning it into dependable carbon storage will require showing that the material can hold its carbon long after the cameras leave.

The study is published in the journal ENGINEERINGenergy.

#6275. An El Niño amped by climate change has California bracing for the worst

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Warming has intensified El Niño’s impacts on weather around the globe, making it harder to prepare

Large waves, driven eastward by the strengthening El Niño in the eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, battered the city of Oceanside California (shown) on October 9.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready. The state has strategically stockpiled sandbags, pumps and generators. Debris has been fished out to clear storm drains, seepage blankets shore up aging levees and dams, and wire mesh cages hold back precariously placed boulders.

What is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves. The fury of this year’s El Niño is being unleashed around the globe as well, from inundating Florida with floods to exacerbating drought in the Amazon. And much more is still to come, forecasts show, with the peak of the climate phenomenon expected to arrive between November 2026 and January 2027.

Californians know all too well the threat. El Niño has historically brought relentless rainfall to the state, flooding cities and triggering landslides.

State officials learned a lot about preparedness and emergency water management from previous El Niños — particularly the strong event that spanned the winter of 1997–1998. But this year’s event is likely to be even more challenging, a “Super” El Niño superimposed on the backdrop of global climate change.

Climate change has made water management in California more complicated than it was just 30 years ago — as it has elsewhere around the world, says environmental scientist Letitia Grenier, the director of water policy at the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonprofit, nonpartisan think tank based in San Francisco.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In 1997, California’s overall climate was much drier; El Niño brought a big, long rainy season that spanned the state, Grenier says. But now, “it’s just so humid. The air is warmer, so it can hold more water.”

That waterlogged atmosphere means that even without El Niño, there’s been less of a distinct rainy season in California, and more rapid flip-flop between intense episodes of rain dumped on the ground followed by periods of heat and dryness. “It’s these strange, erratic patterns that we’ve never seen before,” she says. And the state is bracing for how the Super El Niño will clash with this new climate normal.

1997 was the year that the term “El Niño” shot to global fame. It was the most powerful El Niño in recorded history, and the first to be scientifically monitored in real time, continuously tracked by satellites and breathlessly reported on by news outlets. El Niño’s rise to household name status was even cemented in pop culture by an appearance on Saturday Night Live, in a classic sketch by comedian Chris Farley.

But the event was no laughing matter. It caused global devastation during its brief reign. El Niño events form as westward-blowing trade winds over the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean weaken, allowing warm water to accumulate at the surface. Those waters can then release massive amounts of heat to the atmosphere, altering the position of the Pacific jet stream and helping to disrupt global weather patterns.

In 1997–1998, global temperatures spiked by 1.5 degrees Celsius on average. Along with the torrential rains in California, the event brought brutal drought to Southeast Asia and deadly summer floods to central Europe and Peru. Record-breaking floods also hit East Africa, which in turn triggered a surge in mosquito-borne Rift Valley fever. The oceans were so warm that 16 percent of the world’s reefs died.

In all, the El Niño–related weather extremes were linked to more than 22,000 fatalities around the world, including nearly 200 in the United States, and an estimated $5.7 trillion in global economic losses.

Not every El Niño is equally intense, or impacts weather in quite the same way. “There’s a lot of variability event to event,” says Washington, D.C.–based climate scientist Tom Di Liberto, of the nonprofit climate news organization Climate Central.

But there is a general overall pattern to how El Niño tends to affect weather around the planet, Di Liberto says. For example, there tend to be more tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean, and fewer in the Atlantic — a pattern also observed in 2026.

El Niño also tends to flatten and accelerate the Pacific jet stream, shifting its flow southward, says Mike Anderson, California’s state climatologist for the Department of Water Resources, who is based in Sacramento.  And that has historically meant that a conveyor belt of back-to-back moisture-loaded storms is set on a collision course with the U.S. West Coast.

The El Niño rapidly strengthened during the summer of 2026. As westerly trade winds weakened, warm waters accumulated in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, raising both ocean temperatures and the sea level height (shown in this animation). Red and white colors indicate the highest sea level. Beginning in April and intensifying through November, the El Niño event generated Kelvin waves, massive swells that sweep eastward along the equator toward the Americas.

The 1997–1998 El Niño revealed just how devastating that pattern could be in California.

As much as 30 centimeters inundated parts of the state during the month of February 1998 alone. Storm winds and high surf pounded the coast, while rivers swelled and overtopped their banks. Flooding from the “Groundhog Day Storm” destroyed some 1,700 homes in Bay Area cities Palo Alto and Menlo Park. On February 6 near Rio Nido, about 100 kilometers from San Francisco, a forested hillside suddenly crumbled, sending a wall of mud rushing down the mountain. It destroyed about 30 homes.

Landslides also threatened homes and lives in Southern California.

On February 23, then 25-year-old Jenifer Segraves and her fiancé Glenn Flook were living in an apartment on Laguna Canyon Road, in the city of Laguna Beach. The heavy rains had saturated the neighborhood’s steep hillsides, making the terrain unstable.

“We lived up against a hill in the canyon, so there were stairs up to our apartment,” Segraves says now. “They became like a waterfall. I remember my fiancé carrying me up the stairs because there was so much water.” Segraves called her father, Gary Segraves, in a panic, asking for help. Then, the slope behind the building failed, the apartment flooded and she and Flook fled into the rushing mud.

“We were strong enough to get out, but we were waist-high in mud,” Segraves said. “[My dad] almost drowned getting to us.” All three took shelter at a neighbor’s house, where they showered and hunkered down to wait out the rain.

Around midnight on February 24, the second mudslide arrived.

The neighbor’s “whole house went down,” Segraves says. She escaped through a second-floor window, but her fiancé fell through the floor and was knocked out. He didn’t make it out.

Gary Segraves, meanwhile, was swept down the hillside and landed in a pile of rubble against a rocky cliff. Battered and missing his glasses, he looked around and saw what looked like a doll.

He reached for the little form — and discovered that it was a baby, very cold but alive. Somehow, the 9-month-old had survived being swept out of her crib from a nearby home. The little girl “wouldn’t have survived if he hadn’t picked her up,” Segraves says.

The havoc wreaked across California by the event 30 years ago cast a stark light on the desperate need to expand waterways, maintain infrastructure and coordinate emergency services, Grenier says. “An engineering system can only work as well as its capacity.”

Much of the state’s infrastructure is deteriorating. An October 13 report by the California state auditor noted that the condition of dams and levees across the state “remains a high-risk issue,” with some 57 dams in the state in poor or unsatisfactory condition. “Poorly maintained dams and levees continue to pose a risk to public safety,” the report said.

California’s water management system was also originally designed specifically to simply shunt excess water away from residential areas, rather than try to capture the water or help it infiltrate into aquifers, Grenier says. But that system worked for a different climate, one that wasn’t so prone to “weather whiplash” — wild, sudden swings between extremely wet and extremely dry conditions.

Alongside punishing, drenching back-to-back storms called atmospheric rivers, the state has also experienced frequent episodes of drought, including two recent severe events, one lasting from 2012 to 2016 and another from 2021 to 2025.

Those years of drought, dwindling snow and pumping too much water from aquifers have dramatically depleted the state’s subsurface water stores. And the heavy rains don’t necessarily help; the torrents of water mostly run off across the surface instead of infiltrating soils to reach the underground aquifer.

Such hydroclimate whiplash isn’t unique to California by any means. It’s a global problem, and it’s becoming more common. A small increase in air temperatures can give a big boost to the atmosphere’s capacity to hold water vapor, increasing that capacity by about 7 percent for every 1 degree C of temperature increase. All of that water vapor has contributed to an increase in extreme precipitation events around the globe since the mid-20th century.

Precipitation is just half of the problem. Rising air temperatures also make the air “thirstier,” causing it to draw even more moisture out of vegetation, soil and surface bodies of water during drier periods — which makes the land more vulnerable to severe drought and wildfire.

It’s now clear that these hydrodynamic shifts have been increasing the frequency of weather whiplash events around the world over the last 75 years or so, scientists reported in 2025. And that whiplash is likely to increase as the world warms more.

Months before reaching peak intensity, the 2026–2027 Super El Niño has begun making its presence known. The Amazon is suffering under intense heat and drought, priming the region for wildfires and pushing the forest closer to a worrisome possible fate: a transition from tropical forest to savanna grasslands. Fires have also begun blazing across Southeast Asia, while heavy rains began inundating the Horn of Africa in October. Arriving on the heels of severe drought, that one-two punch could devastate the region’s crops and pasturelands.

In California, the first harbingers of the arrival of the Super El Niño appeared in early September. Heavy surf pounded the coastline. Regions from San Francisco to Los Angeles saw record high tides by late October that flooded city streets and battered coastlines and seawalls, even as the skies remained clear.

The waves were amped up by an unfortunate trifecta: higher sea levels due to climate change; a lunar cycle that exerted its maximum pull on the tides; and an El Niño–linked phenomenon called Kelvin waves.

Kelvin waves are massive, slow-moving swells of warm ocean water, part of the complicated interplay between wind and water that produces the El Niño Southern Oscillation, the overall weather pattern that includes El Niño and counterpart La Niña events, says Josh Willis, an oceanographer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif.

As prevailing west-blowing winds weaken over the tropical eastern Pacific, Willis says, water normally pushed west by the winds instead sloshes back eastward. Kelvin waves have historically given a boost to sea levels along the U.S. West Coast of as much as 30 centimeters. This year, that impact could be larger, researchers reported September 30 in a preprint study posted on EarthArXiv.org. Computer model simulations suggest that the risk of the risk of extreme sea levels could be 10 times higher during this El Niño year than during previous events, for coastlines from Alaska all the way to Chile.

Then, by late October, the Santa Ana winds arrived: Hot, dry gusts blowing down the mountains toward the coast, fanning wildfires in Southern California. The fires scarred the landscape, denuding it of vegetation, roots that helped stabilize and fortify the soil. Such loosened soil is more likely to become mobilized into a debris flow during heavy rains.

Those rains are now on the way. By mid-November, researchers began tracking storms headed for California. The peak of El Niño is expected to arrive by late November or early December and persist through February or March.

Segraves, after surviving nearly 30 years ago, says she is aware that another El Niño is coming. But she hasn’t been following the news closely. She’s placed herself on a news diet since her ordeal. She refused to speak to media for years, or even read the coverage about her own story.

“Everyone wanted to talk to me and I just wanted to be left alone,” she says. Staying away from the news “freed me from all that. It changed my view on life. I take each day as it comes.”

But, she adds, one lesson has stayed with her. “I swore I would never live on a cliff again.”

#6274. Bumblebees May Hold the Secret to How Intelligence Evolved

Bumblebees can solve unfamiliar problems, learn complex skills by watching others, and even transmit emotion-like states to their nestmates. They accomplish all this with fewer than a million neurons, challenging the long-standing assumption that sophisticated intelligence requires a large brain.

In a new Perspective published in Science, researchers Lars Chittka and Stanley Heinze examine growing evidence that advanced cognitive abilities may emerge through evolutionary modifications to ancient neural circuits.

In one experiment, bumblebees learned to move a ball and climb onto it to reach an otherwise inaccessible source of nectar. They could even guide the ball toward a target that was no longer visible, suggesting an ability to mentally represent goals and solve unfamiliar problems.

Another study published in Nature found that bumblebees could learn to open a two-step puzzle box by observing trained nestmates, even though none independently discovered the solution.

Bumblebees also appear capable of transmitting emotion-like states. After receiving an unexpected reward, bees displayed an optimism-like bias when interpreting ambiguous stimuli. Other bees developed a similar bias simply by observing them through a transparent barrier, without physical contact or chemical communication.

“The remarkable cognitive abilities of bees may not have required them to evolve entirely new neural algorithms,” Chittka and Heinze write.

One possible explanation lies in the mushroom bodies, insect brain structures involved in learning and memory. Bumblebees possess approximately 50 times as many specialized neurons called Kenyon cells as fruit flies, giving them greater memory capacity. Additional circuits involved in navigation and decision-making may also allow bees to weigh multiple goals and plan their actions.

“More broadly, higher cognitive processes could have evolved many times and might be more widespread than previously thought,” the authors write.

Scientists have already produced a complete wiring diagram, known as a connectome, of the fruit fly brain. Similar efforts are underway in several bee species. Comparing these neural networks could reveal which evolutionary changes enable sophisticated cognition.

“It seems likely that, just like between birds and mammals, different neural solutions might have evolved to produce similar cognitive traits in different insects,” write the authors. “Both shared and distinct solutions that shape the cognitive abilities of animals might emerge as general principles, and some might apply to both vertebrates and invertebrates.”

Reference: “Bumble bee cognition” by Lars Chittka and Stanley Heinze, 19 November 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.aek1724

#6273. Mindfulness training can backfire at work, and personality may explain why

Mindfulness training may increase negative feelings and rude behavior among employees who already tend to distrust and manipulate others.

Many companies offer mindfulness training in the hope that it will help employees manage stress, get along better and treat each other with kindness. But it doesn’t seem to work that way for everyone.

In a month-long experiment, some workers who practiced mindfulness reported more anger, disgust, and contempt toward coworkers than people with similar personalities in the other groups.

Workers who felt more of this hostility also reported more rudeness at work.

The pattern emerged among employees who scored high on a personality trait called Machiavellianism.

People who score high on this trait tend to distrust others and manipulate them for personal gain. Psychologists group it with two other personality traits under the name dark triad.

Previous research has linked mindfulness to greater empathy and helping coworkers. So why did these employees respond so differently?

The study was led by Adam Kay, an assistant professor in the School of Management at the University of South Florida‘s Muma College of Business.

“Mindfulness training makes us more aware of our thoughts and feelings, but that doesn’t necessarily make us better people,” Kay said.

Kay carried out the experiment at a large North American healthcare organization with 12 hospitals, 90 community health sites and 33 other workplaces.

Six hundred employees volunteered, roughly two-thirds of whom were healthcare professionals. Kay randomly divided them into three groups.

The first group followed a 30-day online mindfulness program. It involved five minutes of daily instruction, along with emails and text messages reminding employees to take five mindful breaths, five times a day.

The idea was simple. Notice the colors around you, listen to nearby sounds or feel your feet touching the floor. Then focus on your breathing and notice your feelings without judging them.

The second group followed a similar breathing exercise without being asked to focus on the present moment. The third group received training later.

After some employees dropped out and others failed attention checks, 473 remained in the study. Before the experiment, they had completed a personality survey containing statements such as “It’s not wise to tell your secrets.”

Three weeks into the experiment, Kay asked employees how often they had felt anger, disgust and contempt toward their coworkers over the previous two weeks.

For people who scored low on Machiavellianism, it barely mattered which group they belonged to.

Things were different for those with high scores. Employees who practiced mindfulness reported stronger negative feelings than people with similar personalities in the other two groups. The difference was moderate.

Interestingly, people in both training groups felt more mindful afterward. Yet the same rise in negative feelings did not occur among those who simply practiced breathing.

Paying closer attention to their inner experiences may have made the difference.

After the program ended, employees answered another survey. This time, Kay wanted to know how they had treated their colleagues during the training.

One statement on the survey read, “I ignored or excluded a colleague from professional camaraderie.”

Psychologists call these small acts of disrespect workplace incivility. They’re often subtle enough that it’s hard to tell whether someone intended to be hurtful.

The more anger, disgust and contempt employees felt, the more rude behavior they reported. This helped explain the link between mindfulness and incivility among workers with Machiavellian traits.

“Workplace incivility isn’t always obvious,” Kay said. “It usually involves subtle acts of disrespect that are easy to dismiss or deny – but that doesn’t make it harmless.”

More obvious forms of mistreatment, such as embarrassing someone in front of other coworkers, did not follow the same pattern.

“That workplace incivility can be so damaging yet so difficult to pin on perpetrators may be precisely why it appeals to Machiavellians, who tend to be calculating and reputation-conscious,” Kay said.

Imagine working alongside someone you secretly dislike. Most days, you’re too busy answering emails, attending meetings or finishing your work to give those feelings much thought.

Now you spend part of every day paying attention to your thoughts and emotions. You may begin to notice just how much you dislike that person.

Kay suspects something similar happened during the experiment. Mindfulness may not have created those negative feelings. Instead, it may have made existing ones harder to ignore.

The paper even opens with a reference to philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche’s famous observation about staring into an abyss that stares back at you.

Kay considered several other possibilities. Employees were not spending more time dwelling on angry thoughts, hiding their emotions or viewing their colleagues as less than human.

A bad mood didn’t explain the findings either. Neither did the other two dark triad traits, narcissism and psychopathy.

This isn’t the first time researchers have discovered unexpected effects of mindfulness. Earlier research found that it can reduce people’s motivation to repair damaged relationships.

Machiavellianism is a personality trait that exists to varying degrees in the general population. Companies could encounter similar problems in almost any workplace.

Instead, companies could pay closer attention to how employees treat one another after completing a program. Lower stress and better productivity aren’t the only outcomes worth measuring.

Programs that teach compassion and ethical behavior alongside mindfulness might help. However, the people who could benefit most from such lessons may also be the least interested in taking them.

There’s an important limitation to this research. Everything Kay learned about the employees’ feelings and behavior came from the employees themselves.

Perhaps mindfulness simply made some workers more willing to admit that they had been rude. Although Kay protected their anonymity, he cannot completely dismiss that possibility.

He considers it less likely because the pattern appeared only among workers with high Machiavellian scores who practiced mindfulness, and only for subtle acts of disrespect.

The experiment also took place at a single healthcare organization and used a commercial mindfulness program that hasn’t been independently tested.

Hospitals have strict rules about professional behavior, which may discourage more obvious forms of hostility.

Future studies could ask coworkers whether they noticed changes in behavior. Researchers could also observe employees directly or test different mindfulness programs.

“Mindfulness training can bring our darker feelings into sharper focus,” Kay said. “And sometimes, it’s our coworkers who pay the price.”

Learning to recognize our feelings and learning to treat others better are two different things. Mindfulness may help with the first without necessarily improving the second.

The study is published in the Journal of Business Ethics.

Archaeological discoveries can offer remarkable insights into the lives, cultures and beliefs of ancient peoples. From richly furnished royal tombs to caches of silver coins, some of the most significant finds have revealed how people lived, traded, fought, governed and died thousands of years ago.

Other discoveries stand out for their extraordinary preservation or historical significance. For example, the most expensive shipwreck on record — the 300-year-old Spanish galleon San José that's worth an estimated $17 billion — was found off the coast of Colombia in 2015 and continues to inform archaeologists and challenge governments that can't agree about its modern ownership. The Rosetta stone opened up the world of ancient Egypt to scholars, but researchers are still trying to decipher the mysterious Indus Valley script, one of the world's earliest urban civilizations.

#6271. Paleontologists Discover a Hidden Ecosystem Surrounding a 9.5-Million-Year-Old Whale

A 9.5-million-year-old fossil discovery suggests that an ecological relationship observed in modern oceans has ancient origins.

A whale that sank to the bottom of an ancient sea approximately 9.5 million years ago may have attracted a community of marine scavengers. Scientists excavating fossil deposits in southern Denmark have discovered microscopic skeletal plates that belong to a previously unknown species of brittle star, a marine invertebrate closely related to starfish.

Named Ophiura huebnerjenseni, the species may provide the earliest fossil evidence of brittle stars gathering around dead whales. Such carcasses create temporary ecosystems known as whale falls, supplying abundant food to organisms living on the seafloor. Brittle stars frequently inhabit these environments today, but their association with whale falls had never been documented in the fossil record.

The remains were recovered from sediment collected during the 2018 excavation of a beaked whale’s lower jaw and several vertebrae at Denmark’s Gram Clay Pit. Researchers washed and sieved the sediment before examining individual microfossils using scanning electron microscopy. Subtle differences in the structure of the brittle stars’ skeletal plates allowed the team to identify a new species.

The distribution of the fossils suggested that their proximity to the whale was more than coincidental.

“Only three samples taken directly beside the whale bones contained brittle-star remains. Samples from the same layer farther from the skeleton, and other comparison samples, yielded none,” the lead author Ben Thuy explains.

The researchers investigated whether ocean currents or favorable fossil preservation conditions could explain the unusual concentration of skeletal plates. Fragments of sea urchins, which have similar physical and chemical properties, provided a useful comparison.

“We considered whether currents had simply concentrated the plates around the bones, or whether local chemical conditions had helped preserve them. However, sea-urchin fragments of comparable size and mineral composition occurred in every sample studied. This makes a preservation-only explanation less likely and supports the interpretation that the brittle stars lived on or close to the whale carcass,” Thuy added.

The Gram Clay Pit preserves sediments deposited beneath the ancient North Sea during the Late Miocene. Although the site has yielded numerous whale skeletons, exceptionally large megalodon vertebrae, and a diverse collection of marine invertebrates, brittle stars had previously escaped detection.

A decomposing whale delivers a substantial supply of organic material to the seabed. In modern oceans, whale falls can support successive communities of scavengers, opportunistic invertebrates, and, particularly in deep water, organisms sustained by chemical processes associated with decomposition.

Although the fossils cannot establish what Ophiura huebnerjenseni ate or whether it depended on whale carcasses, researchers suspect it was a generalist species that normally occupied the surrounding seabed and congregated where food became abundant.

“We interpret the site as a shallow-water whale fall at a stage when enrichment from the carcass supported opportunistic animals,” said Mette Elstrup. “We found no evidence for the later sulfide-based community stages that can develop at deep-sea whale falls. The discovery therefore adds a rare fossil perspective on how animals responded to a large food source on an ancient shallow-water seabed,” Elstrup said.

The new species takes its name from Holger Hübner and Thomas Jensen, founders of Germany’s Wacken Open Air heavy metal festival. The connection extends beyond the scientific tribute, however, to the geological origins of the festival’s famously muddy grounds.

Researchers believe the dark gray mud encountered by festivalgoers probably originates from the same geological deposits that preserved the ancient brittle stars.

“The clay that accumulated on the bottom of the ancient North Sea not only preserved the remains of a 9.5-million-years old brittle star, it also turns Wacken Open Air into the muddy battlefield renowned by metalheads worldwide,” concludes Lea Numberger-Thuy.

Reference: “A new brittle star (Ophiuroidea, Ophiuridae) associated with a whale fall from the Miocene of Gram, Denmark” by Ben Thuy, Mette Elstrup, Lea D. Numberger-Thuy and Trine Sørensen, 19 October 2026, Neues Jahrbuch für Geologie und Paläontologie – Abhandlungen. DOI: 10.1127/njgpa/2026/1335

#6270. Habits like nail biting may be clues to hidden mental health struggles in teens

About one in eight students surveyed in England reported significant distress over nail biting, skin picking, or hair pulling.

Nail biting and skin picking are widely regarded as nothing more serious than bad habits. In a survey of students in England, most teens who reported these behaviors said they caused little or no distress.

The survey was answered by 5,437 students. More than half of them reported sometimes picking, pulling, or biting at their hair, skin, or nails.

The behavior was described as difficult to control, although little or no distress was reported by most of these students.

About one in eight students gave a different answer. These students said the behavior upset them quite a lot or a great deal. This distress was closely associated with anxiety, depression, and bullying.

The study was led by Clare Mackay, a professor in the Department of Psychiatry at the University of Oxford. The behaviors are familiar to her from her own life.

Researchers have a name for them: body-focused repetitive behaviors, or BFRBs.

“BFRBs aren’t simply bad habits. They’re often signs that a young person is struggling,” Mackay said.

Because the students were surveyed only once, the answers can indicate which problems occur together. The order in which those problems appeared cannot be established from the data.

The questions formed part of the 2025 OxWell Student Survey, which reached 32,102 students in England.

A total of 49 secondary schools and colleges took part, and most were state schools in Oxfordshire and Merseyside.

The survey was usually completed online during a lesson. An optional set of questions was then offered, and some students continued to it.

Within that group, the questions about picking, pulling, and biting were answered by 5,437 students aged 11 to 18.

Three questions were written for the survey by Mackay’s team. Before being sent to schools, the questions were tried by 26 people with personal experience of the behaviors. Those people also commented on the questions.

In the first question, students were asked about picking, pulling, or biting at hair, skin, or nails. Only behavior that feels difficult to control was covered by this question.

In the second question, students were asked how much the behavior upset them. Four possible answers were offered, ranging from not at all to a great deal.

The third question asked whether the behavior interfered with home life, friendships, leisure activities, or classroom learning.

Overall, at least one such behavior was reported by 58.5% of the students. Nail biting was the most common at 43.6%. It was followed by skin picking at 31.3% and by hair pulling at 14.5%.

For most of these students, the behavior was not experienced as a source of distress.

Among students who reported a behavior, 35.2% said it didn’t upset them at all. Another 42.6% said it upset them only a little. One of the two highest distress ratings was chosen by the other 22.2%.

The researchers then focused on that smaller group. It was made up of 691 students, or 12.7% of everyone surveyed. The highest rating was chosen by 182 of them.

The lowest levels of distress were reported by students who only bit their nails. One of the two highest distress ratings was chosen by 11% of them.

The share was 29% among students who picked their skin. Among students who pulled their hair, a share of 37% was recorded.

Hair pulling and skin picking are listed as disorders in psychiatry’s diagnostic manuals. No separate category has been given to nail biting.

Considerable overlap between the behaviors was also observed.

At least one other behavior was reported by 84% of the students who pulled their hair. Among students who picked their skin, the corresponding figure was 76%.

The authors suggested that the behaviors may share one underlying process. On this account, they may not be separate conditions.

Interference with daily life was also reported more often for hair pulling than for nail biting.

Depending on the area of life, interference was reported by 5% to 13% of students who only bit their nails. For students who pulled their hair, the range was 18% to 39%.

At least one behavior was reported by 45.6% of boys and 64.6% of girls.

A third group consisted of 272 students who identified as trans or gender diverse, or who were unsure. Within that group, a share of 84.2% was recorded.

Distress was also lowest among boys. Distressing behaviors were reported by 5.6% of boys and 16.4% of girls. In the trans, gender-diverse, or unsure group, the figure was 25%.

The team then accounted for anxiety, depression, bullying, and age. The gaps between boys and the other two groups remained.

In studies of adults seen in clinics, about four women have been reported for every man with these conditions. A much smaller gap between girls and boys was observed among the students.

According to Mackay’s team, these behaviors had not previously been reported in trans and gender-diverse adolescents.

A standard 25-question checklist of anxiety and depression symptoms was also completed by the students.

Distressing behaviors were reported by 6.3% of students whose scores fell in the normal range. The share was 19.4% in the borderline range. In the highest range, which is labeled clinical by the checklist, it was 34.2%.

Distressing behaviors were also more common among students who reported bullying.

Among students who reported no recent bullying, 9.6% had distressing behaviors. A share of 27.1% was recorded among students bullied about once a week or more.

The team then analyzed these factors together. Anxiety and depression symptoms showed the strongest link to distressing behaviors. Gender and frequent bullying also remained linked.

Distressing behaviors were reported about twice as often by students who said they had autism, ADHD, or both. The comparison was made with students who reported neither condition.

Once anxiety, depression, gender, and bullying had been accounted for, that difference was no longer statistically significant.

The authors wrote that picking, pulling, and biting may work as a way of managing difficult feelings. The behaviors can then become a source of shame.

Young people may stay silent about the behaviors because of shame and stigma, said Polly Waite. For the same reasons, help may not be requested.

Waite is a co-author from Oxford’s Department of Experimental Psychology.

That question cannot be answered by the survey. Since each student answered only once, it cannot be shown whether anxiety leads to picking and pulling.

It is also possible that anxiety is increased by the behaviors.

Earlier work suggests that the relationship may run in both directions.

The students also may not represent English teenagers as a whole. Participation in the optional questions was a matter of choice.

Compared with the full survey, this group included more girls and gender-diverse students. Higher anxiety and depression scores were recorded in it as well.

As a result, students with emotional difficulties may have been over-counted.

The three questions are new and have not yet been formally tested. It also cannot be determined from them which students would meet the criteria for a diagnosis.

Mackay’s team wrote that these behaviors are rarely asked about in schools and clinics. A single screening question was therefore suggested by the authors.

It asks whether picking, pulling, or biting upsets a young person. It also asks whether the behavior stops them from doing things they want to do.

The next question is whether distress tied to these behaviors would be eased by reducing anxiety, depression, or bullying.

The authors wrote that this could be tested in future studies, especially among girls and gender-diverse young people.

The full study was published in the journal BMJ Mental Health.

#6269. The libido drug women want is testosterone

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The FDA has yet to approve a testosterone product for female libido. That hasn’t stopped demand

One urologist says she has seen testosterone therapy for female libido "change people’s lives." But the data — and regulators — still need to catch up.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

These days, Jessica Yih spends a lot of time talking to women about testosterone. Interest is “coming from all directions,” says the University of California, Irvine Health urologist. A major source: women who hope testosterone can boost the female libido. Only about a decade ago, women looking for libido treatments had few medical options — even though women of all ages struggle with low sexual desire.

Some non-hormonal treatments are now available, but the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has yet to approve a female testosterone product, despite years of research suggesting it can boost sexual function and desire among postmenopausal women. Female testosterone products are approved in countries including the United Kingdom and Australia.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Not many studies have looked at testosterone’s effects on libido in premenopausal women, but preliminary data in that area are also promising, according to a 2026 research review in The Journal of Sexual Medicine that Yih coauthored. “I have seen it change people’s lives,” Yih says. The hormone seems to make the female brain more receptive to sexual stimuli; it also promotes physical effects that enhance sexual pleasure, such as increased blood flow to the genitals. Right now, American women interested in these potential benefits have to look for them off-label. But that may change. In September, the FDA held a public meeting on testosterone use among menopausal women, “with the goal of informing future research and potential drug development in this area,” says Kaveeta Vasisht, the FDA’s associate commissioner for women’s health.

The hormone has a rocky regulatory past. In 2004, an FDA advisory panel unanimously voted against approving a testosterone patch for women, citing a lack of safety data. There are still outstanding questions on that front, Yih says—like how, if at all, long-term use affects risk of conditions such as breast cancer and heart disease. Then, in 2011, a pair of Phase III trials found that testosterone therapy didn’t significantly outperform a placebo — a benchmark the FDA looks for when deciding whether to approve a new drug. That’s not to say testosterone didn’t work, says Tami Rowen, an ob-gyn at UC San Francisco. Rather, it seemed that hype about the hormone was so strong that study participants went in with sky-high expectations, leading even the placebo group to report benefits. The treatment was a “victim of its own success,” Rowen says.

Interest hasn’t let up, though. By one estimate, the U.S. female prescription rate for all uses rose from 0.4 out of every 1,000 women in 2018, to 1.8 out of every 1,000 women in 2026. That’s an increase of nearly 400 percent. With so much buzz, the potential placebo effect remains “the biggest problem with testosterone right now,” Rowen says.

Another outstanding question, Yih says, is whether using testosterone long-term increases the risk of breast cancer and heart disease.

Women seeking a libido boost do have non-hormonal options. In 2015, the FDA approved Addyi, the first treatment for low libido in premenopausal women. The drug seemingly raises levels of neurotransmitters that promote sexual desire while tamping down those that block it. A competitor, Vyleesi, hit shelves in 2019. Then, last year, regulators expanded Addyi’s use to postmenopausal women younger than 65. An international group of experts, including Rowen, issued recommendations for treating low female libido in 2025 in Sexual Medicine Reviews. Psychological therapies and Addyi are backed by the strongest evidence, the group found.

Rowen currently has her eye on in-development products including Lybrido. The drug, which is slated to enter a Phase III clinical trial in Europe, aims to rev sex drive in the brain and enhance physical arousal. The demand for new treatments is there, Rowen says. “Women deserve better than placebo.”

#6268. Ancient hunters in Australia had more on the menu than archaeologists expected

Ancient bones from two sites in northwestern Australia suggest that a varied diet gave hunters more options as rainfall and prey availability changed.

Ancient hunters in northwestern Australia ate a wide range of animals, and their leftovers suggest they could be choosy.

A study spanning roughly 50,000 years found that dietary variety could reflect plentiful food and skilled hunting.

The research was led by Tiina Manne from the University of Queensland. Her team examined ancient animal remains from Riwi rockshelter and Boodie Cave on Barrow Island.

A widely used archaeological model predicts that hunters first concentrate on prey offering the greatest returns. They add less rewarding animals when preferred foods become harder to obtain.

The new research challenges that reading of dietary diversity. At both Australian sites, people ate many kinds of animals from early in the occupation records.

“First Nations peoples in Australia were much more sophisticated and strategic in the animals they chose to hunt,” Manne said.

“Flexibility, not fixation on a few species of prey, was the smartest way to live in an unpredictable climate.”

Riwi stands on Gooniyandi traditional lands near the Great Sandy Desert. People began using the rockshelter about 45,000 years ago.

Its deposits contain remains of wallabies, echidnas, possums, flying foxes, lizards, and snakes. Small wallabies, lizards, and snakes dominate the earliest part of the analyzed sequence.

Boodie Cave’s first occupation dates to between about 51,100 and 46,200 years ago. Barrow Island was then part of the mainland, with its surroundings changing as sea levels fell and rose.

The team identified 1,167 specimens from Riwi and 2,083 from Boodie Cave by animal group or body size. The varied diets persisted across substantial environmental changes.

Burned bones and impact marks at Riwi helped link the remains to human food preparation. Some fractures also occurred while the bones were fresh.

“In a land of unpredictable rainfall, a variety of foods signal ‘plenty’, and flexibility was the best strategy,” Manne explained.

Some of the most revealing findings were bones still joined together, known as articulated remains. Their condition suggested that people had discarded body parts with little nutritional value.

“On Barrow Island, which was then connected to the mainland, the diet included wallabies, turtles and reef fish, and articulated bones suggest only the most nutritious parts were eaten and the rest were discarded,” Manne said.

“This isn’t the behavior of people short of food – they could afford to be choosy, so a broad diet reflected choice, not scarcity.”

The paper dates these articulated remains to around 7,200–6,800 years ago, long after the earliest occupation. Around this time, rising seas were cutting Barrow Island off from the mainland.

The researchers documented 24 groups of joined bones, including fish spines and parts of turtle limbs.

They interpret these discarded portions as evidence that people could select the more rewarding parts of their catches.

An animal’s value depended on more than its size. Weather affected both its condition and the effort needed to catch it.

“When water and vegetation were plentiful, large kangaroos were spread thin across the landscape, but in arid conditions they became easier to ambush as they stayed near waterholes,” Manne said.

“Small animals like bandicoots were also a good option when it got dry, because they stayed fat by switching to eating insects.”

“Hunters who kept their options open could shift between prey as conditions changed.”

At Riwi, large kangaroo remains became prominent after about 34,000 years ago, as conditions grew drier. The authors suggest hunting them became less risky when water drew the animals into more predictable locations.

Fat mattered, too. Opened leg bones at both sites point to the extraction of marrow, while smaller insect-eating animals could retain valuable fat during drought.

Many Australian animals hide in burrows, vegetation, or rock crevices during the day. Finding them requires knowing which traces to follow.

The paper draws on First Nations ecological knowledge, including signs such as fresh tracks, disturbed soil, and scratches on bark. These can reveal prey that a hunter cannot see directly.

“A tremendous amount of ecological knowledge is passed on in oral histories, including subtle signs of not only how to find prey, but the best prey depending on the season and circumstances,” Manne said.

Where hidden animals were abundant and diverse, investigating those signs could reward hunters with many different foods. A smaller animal could be a dependable catch even when a larger one promised more meat.

The authors argue that archaeological diets need to be understood through local animal behavior, food availability, and hunting costs.

A fixed ranking of desirable prey can miss how those factors change with rainfall.

Animal remains also reveal only part of a meal. Plant foods, documented at other northern Australian sites, would have supplied important carbohydrates alongside meat and fat.

“Importantly, our work suggests archaeologists around the world should re-consider how they have interpreted diet choice and diversity,” Manne concluded.

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the Natural Academy of Sciences.

The BepiColombo spacecraft has overcome a last-minute computer glitch to enter orbit around Mercury — the 2nd craft in history to orbit the closest planet to the sun.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Update: On Tuesday (Nov. 24) ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher announced on X that the BepiColombo team has isolated the computer glitch, and tweaked the mission accordingly. "The remaining manoeuvres have already been replanned, with no extra burns needed," Aschbacher said. The two probes are still on track to seprate on Dec. 9. (This article was updated at 11:40 a.m. ET on Nov. 24).

After eight years slingshotting around the inner solar system, the joint European-Japanese spacecraft BepiColombo has finally entered into orbit around Mercury — becoming only the second mission ever to orbit the closest planet to the sun.

Mission scientists confirmed on Saturday (Nov. 21) that the spacecraft reached Mercury's orbit and is transmitting data back to the ground team.

However, the orbital insertion didn't go entirely as planned, European Space Agency (ESA) representatives said in a statement on Monday. Due to a software glitch, the spacecraft didn't fire its thrusters for the full 37 minutes required to slow its approach to Mercury.

ESA has investigates the issue and confirmed the spacecraft's new trajectory; meanwhile, BepiColombo remains "safe," the statement noted. The spacecraft should be ready to begin a year of intensive science observations of Mercury starting a few months from now.

An illustration of BepiColombo approaching Mercury for orbital insertion.

Built jointly by ESA and the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), BepiColombo is actually two separate probes, which are currently stacked one atop the other in orbit. The ESA-built orbiter, named the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), and the JAXA-built orbiter, the Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (Mio), carry separate science instruments, and they will soon diverge into separate orbital paths around the mysterious inner planet, operating as two probes gathering different streams of data.

A selfie of BepiColombo during a flyby of Mercury's north pole in 2025.

The pair of probes launched together aboard an Ariane 5 rocket in October 2018, and spent the following eight years on an interplanetary journey that took them past Earth, the moon and Venus. It even passed by Mercury itself six times. (During one of these flybys, in January 2025, Bepi snapped an incredible closeup photo of Mercury's north pole.)

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

This complicated cosmic choreography was necessary to prevent BepiColombo from picking up too much speed and overshooting Mercury's orbit, according to ESA. Mercury sits about 36 million miles (58 million kilometers) from our star, or roughly one third of the distance between Earth and the sun. That makes it very difficult for a spacecraft to reach Mercury without being captured by the sun's considerable gravitational pull and dragged off course.

Only one other spacecraft — NASA's MESSENGER probe — has succeeded in entering Mercury orbit before, circling the planet from 2011 to 2015 after its own seven-year journey through space.

BepiColombo will spend the next few months getting both probes in position to start mapping Mercury in the greatest detail ever.

MPO and Mio are expected to separate in early December, with Mio entering a highly elliptical orbit around Mercury's poles. MPO will then take a few more months to fine-tune its trajectory, reaching a lower and more circular polar orbit in March 2027, according to ESA. Its science operations are expected to begin in April.

The sibling probes will each orbit Mercury several times a day, with MPO completing an orbit every 2 hours or so. Observing the mysterious inner planet from several different vantage points, the probes will make the most comprehensive map of Mercury ever. The mission's suite of science instruments will study the planet across the electromagnetic spectrum, taking observations in X-rays, gamma-rays and ultraviolet light, as well as collecting detailed measurements of the planet's magnetic field.

With this information, scientists hope to unravel many mysteries of the least-explored planet in the solar system. The new data should enable scientists to tackle myriad long-standing questions: What is Mercury's interior made of, and where does its magnetic field come from? How was the planet formed, and to what extent is it still tectonically active today? By making precise measurements of the spacecraft's orbit and position, a radio experiment will also provide a new test of Einstein's theory of general relativity.

Stay tuned for more updates from ESA about humanity's first visit to Mercury in more than a decade.

#6266. Virtual reality can make you feel sick even when the scene around you stays still

In a five-minute VR experiment, watching a single moving ball increased nausea, eye discomfort, and disorientation as the eyes aimed and focused at different distances.

Volunteers spent five minutes in a virtual reality headset watching a speckled ball glide toward them and away against a black background. Afterward, they reported more nausea, eye discomfort, and disorientation than before.

The ball was designed to put two jobs the eyes normally do together at odds.

As it appeared to move closer, the volunteers’ eyes turned inward to follow it, but the headset kept the image in focus at a fixed distance.

A cap of 64 electrodes recorded their brain activity shifting while it happened.

The research was conducted by Mattie Johnson, a computer science doctoral student at the University of Maryland.

Amitabh Varshney, a computer science professor and dean at the university, led the study, and Sujal Bista of the University of Maryland Institute for Health Computing was a co-author.

The team worked with the Food and Drug Administration and Sony on the study.

The team is careful about what the electrode readings mean. The scene used for comparison differed from the test scene in more than one way, and the authors can’t fully rule out eye and facial muscle activity.

So the paper calls the brain changes candidate correlates, not a signature of this kind of sickness.

Look at a real object and your eyes do two things at once: they turn inward to aim at it, and their lenses adjust to bring it into focus.

The two distances agree. A headset breaks the agreement. Its screens sit at one fixed focal distance while the 3D picture asks the eyes to aim nearer or farther.

The Meta Quest 2 used here has its focal plane about 4.3 feet (1.3 meters) in front of the eyes. The team measured that with a camera and a test pattern.

Within about half a diopter of that distance the mismatch is mild. Outside it, discomfort builds.

So the team showed volunteers a black-and-white speckled ball on a black background. It glided from 11 inches (0.275 meters) out to 4.7 feet (1.425 meters) and back, one round trip every 3.9 seconds.

The ball grew as it receded and shrank as it approached, so it always looked the same size.

The researchers designed the scene to reduce the feeling that viewers themselves were moving while still making their eyes aim nearer and farther.

Forty people, 65% of them men and nearly all between 18 and 30, took part.

The researchers analyzed brain recordings from 38 people and complete questionnaires from 38 people. Each analysis excluded a different pair of participants.

Each person sat through five minutes with eyes closed, five minutes looking at a headset’s static home screen, and then five minutes of the moving ball.

Before and after the ball, they filled out a 1993 simulator sickness questionnaire, the SSQ. It scores nausea, eye-related symptoms, and disorientation.

All three scores rose, and the total score rose by what statisticians call a large effect. Men and women both reported more symptoms, though men’s disorientation scores didn’t rise by a reliable amount.

Most participants described themselves as not at all or only slightly prone to this kind of sickness.

The electrode cap sampled the scalp 250 times a second. Software stripped out blinks and muscle noise as best it could.

The team compared 50 seconds of brain activity near the end of the home-screen baseline with 50 seconds near the end of the moving-ball scene.

In clusters of activity toward the front of the head, power in the fast beta and gamma brain waves fell. In clusters toward the back, power in the slower theta waves fell.

“In the frontal lobe, we found a statistically significant decrease in high brain wave frequencies during cybersickness, and in the occipital lobe we saw a statistically significant decrease in low brain wave frequencies,” Johnson said.

“These changes in what we call EEG clusters could be useful predictors of a cybersickness experience.”

The pattern is not the one Varshney’s group found in 2022 for the motion kind of virtual reality sickness, where slower waves grew stronger over the center of the head.

The studies found different patterns, but the researchers still don’t know whether the latest pattern reflects sickness, differences between the scenes, or both.

The baseline scene and the ball differed in brightness, content, and layout. Volunteers were told where to look during the ball but not during the baseline.

Some of the drop in slow waves at the back of the head may simply be visual processing of a different picture. The front of the head is also where eye movements leak into recordings most.

The team didn’t record whether participants wore glasses or contacts, and nearly everyone was under 30.

The authors also wrote that the headset’s three fixed lens-spacing settings fit a larger share of women than men poorly. That could add to symptoms in ways the study can’t separate.

Whether the brain changes track the sickness itself, the change of scenery, or both is the question the authors leave open.

Settling it would need a baseline scene matched to the test scene, which the authors recommend. It would also need eye tracking to remove the eyes’ own electrical traces, which Johnson’s team plans to add.

The goal beyond that is a headset that detects the pattern and adjusts the scene.

“Ultimately we want to inform technology to mitigate symptoms in real time, improving user comfort and productivity over extended periods of immersion,” Johnson said.

Bista put it as a shift in who gets asked.

“The SSQ still has its uses, but now we have the tools to go from asking participants how they’re feeling to asking the brain and body what’s really going on,” he said.

The full study was published in the journal Virtual Reality.
